catalog_quote: [Firchow, Firchow & Akoitai 1973: viii] 2.3 STRESS (or ACCENT). Simplified rules of stress are as follows: 2.3.1 TWO OR THREE SYLLABLES Rule: The first syllable is stressed. kepa 'house' ito 'banana' utave 'baylor shell' 2.3.2 FOUR SYLLABLES Rule: The first and third syllables are stressed. etokasi 'fire' atarito 'fish' 2.3.3 FIVE OR MORE SYLLABLES Rule: The third from the last syllable is stressed most strongly. garutuvira 'slowly' popotepairara 'white men' 2.3.4. EXCEPTIONS. The above rules are complicated by the occurrence of long vowels, and the third rule does not always hold true in some longer verb constructions. [Robinson 2011: 31-33] One such class of exceptions are bisyllabic words in which the first syllable consists of a single short vowel and the second syllable consists of a single long vowel ... In these words, primary stress falls on the second syllable rather than the f…

audit.reasoning: (1) Both deciding quotations verified verbatim in copies we hold at the stated locators (Firchow et al. 1973 p. viii sec. 2.3.1-2.3.4 page scan; Robinson 2011 sec. 3.2.2 pp. 31-34 incl. (8) and Tables 3.8-3.11). (2) The classification 'weight-hedged / quantity-sensitive trochaic, left edge, heavy=CVV' rests on Robinson's 2011 dissertation reanalysis plus the 1973 SIL vocabulary note; these are the best available descriptions - the remaining Glottolog grammar items (Firchow 1974 ms. grammar, Firchow 1970/1987) were downloaded now and are silent on stress (1974's phonology chapter is an outline that defers to the 1973 introduction), and the 1992 SIL OPD, also downloaded, says only 'Stress is probably not phonemic', which is consistent with rule-governed stress. sources.quote: 'Stress is probably not phonemic.' (long vowels /ii ee aa oo uu/ listed as phonemic; syllable patterns V, VV, CV, CVV). Consistent with predictable (rule-governed) stress; gives no location rule.

sources.citation: Firchow, Irwin B. 1974. Rotokas grammar. Unpublished manuscript, SIL, Ukarumpa. 188 pp. [Glottolog 'grammar', 181 pp]
sources.quote: Chapter Two Phonology is an unfilled outline: '(This chapter will be based upon the Rotokas Phonemic Statement written to fulfill the PNG Branch of SIL requirement and the paper ... for Anthropological Linguistics December 1969 ... The practical section dealing with pronunciation with examples will be taken from the introduction to the lexicon of Rotokas-Pidgin-English published by SIL in 1973. Following the body of the chapter will be drills ... mainly to help with stress and length.)' No stress rule of its own; it defers to the 1973 introduction we already quote.

tone.quote: Typological and structural characteristics of the languages of the West Bougainville Stock include extremely simple segmental phonologies with very small segmental phoneme inventories. For instance, the phoneme inventory of Rotokas (Firchow 1969) is as follows: [consonant and vowel chart] One very unusual feature is the lack of nasal consonants. At the same time, in Rotokas at least, there is a complex suprasegmental phonology in which length and stress patterns play a part.
